{
  "proposals": [
    {
      "title": "PinT-AIMD: Parallel-in-time ab initio molecular dynamics for water",
      "field": "computational chemistry / molecular dynamics",
      "sequential_part": "Born-Oppenheimer MD advances nuclear positions one timestep at a time; each SCF wavefunction optimization waits on the previous nuclear geometry and electron density.",
      "restructure": "Use Parareal/MGRIT in time with a coarse semi-empirical propagator and fine GPU DFT propagators; evaluate independent fine time-slices in parallel as GPU batches, then iterate the time grid until the trajectory correction converges.",
      "condition": "Fine electronic-structure cost dominates over communication; the coarse model is accurate enough over short time intervals; trajectory statistics tolerate parallel-in-time correction or a short chaotic horizon.",
      "baselines": "Standard serial CPU/GPU Born-Oppenheimer MD in CP2K or VASP for the same system; check radial distribution functions, velocity autocorrelation, energy drift, and RMSD.",
      "first_test": "Run 32 water molecules for 1000 steps with a semi-empirical coarse propagator on one GPU; measure the first 10 Parareal iterations against the serial trajectory. Rough cost: about 1 GPU-hour."
    },
    {
      "title": "Anti-diagonal tiled Smith-Waterman for long-read candidate filtering",
      "field": "genomics / bioinformatics",
      "sequential_part": "Smith-Waterman dynamic programming has a wavefront dependency: each cell needs its north, west, and north-west neighbors, so the fill is inherently anti-diagonal sequential.",
      "restructure": "Reformulate the algorithm as tiled wavefront kernels on a GPU: process anti-diagonals of tiles, keep boundary cells in shared memory, pack multiple queries per thread block, and shard a reference database across GPUs.",
      "condition": "Long reads and many candidate alignments keep all streaming multiprocessors busy; tile size fits shared memory; scoring and traceback can be separated so traceback does not serialize the whole kernel.",
      "baselines": "Farrar striped Smith-Waterman with AVX2, CUDASW++ 3.0, and Parasail on CPU/GPU; compare exact scores, CIGAR strings, and GCUPS on the same dataset.",
      "first_test": "Align 100k 5kb reads to a 10 Mbp reference on one GPU; record GCUPS and score matches against the CPU baseline. Rough cost: about $5-10 of GPU time."
    },
    {
      "title": "Lockstep many-chain MCMC with batched GPU likelihoods for scientific regression",
      "field": "Bayesian statistics / scientific inference",
      "sequential_part": "A single Markov chain is sequential: each proposal depends on the previous accept/reject decision and target density.",
      "restructure": "Run thousands of independent chains in lockstep GPU batches; vectorize the target log-density over chains and data; keep warmup and adaptation synchronized, then aggregate posterior diagnostics from all chains.",
      "condition": "The model can be expressed as elementwise or matrix operations broadcast over chains and data; GPU memory is sufficient for the batch state; chains are independent enough that synchronization overhead remains small.",
      "baselines": "Stan single-chain CPU/GPU, PyMC or JAX GPU sampler, and a naive multi-core chain implementation; compare ESS/sec, R-hat, and posterior quantiles.",
      "first_test": "Logistic regression with 100k rows and moderate dimensionality, using 256 chains on one GPU; measure ESS/sec and R-hat against one serial chain. Rough cost: about 1 GPU-hour."
    },
    {
      "title": "Sparse event-driven cortical microcircuit on a GPU",
      "field": "computational neuroscience",
      "sequential_part": "Neurons update step by step, and spikes must be delivered at later timesteps; event queues and synaptic current accumulation have serial ordering constraints.",
      "restructure": "Use a fixed-step GPU loop with parallel neuron updates, delayed ring buffers for spikes, atomic synaptic accumulation, and compressed sparse adjacency; optionally keep the small sequential control loop on the CPU while heavy synaptic kernels run on the GPU.",
      "condition": "The network is large and sparse with low firing rates; synaptic count dominates neuron count; communication and atomic contention remain below the kernel compute cost.",
      "baselines": "NEST or Brian2 single-thread CPU simulation, and GeNN where available, for an identical network; compare spike trains using the van Rossum distance, firing rates, and wall time.",
      "first_test": "Simulate 100k Izhikevich neurons with 1M random sparse synapses for 1 second of biological time on one GPU; compare spike count and runtime with the CPU baseline. Rough cost: about 5-10 GPU-min after build."
    },
    {
      "title": "Space-time parallel multigrid for shallow-water ocean dynamics",
      "field": "climate / ocean modeling",
      "sequential_part": "Explicit time stepping is CFL-limited: each grid update waits on the previous timestep, so long horizons serialize millions of small steps.",
      "restructure": "Apply MGRIT or space-time multigrid on GPUs: split the time domain into chunks run on separate GPU streams or tiles, solve corrections on a coarse time grid, and iterate until the result matches serial accuracy.",
      "condition": "The problem is large enough to amortize iteration overhead; the coarse time integrator is stable or diffusive enough for hyperbolic modes; the convergence factor is bounded so parallel speedup exceeds serial execution.",
      "baselines": "A single-GPU or MPI domain-decomposed shallow-water solver and a verified time-marching reference; compare mass and energy conservation and RMS field error.",
      "first_test": "Run 2D wave propagation or a double-gyre at 256x256 for 1000 steps; compare five Parareal iterations with the serial reference. Rough cost: about 1-2 GPU-hours."
    }
  ]
}
